content: A group of experts was assembled to assist in the development of this guideline (Annex 5). This group included individuals who had previously participated in various WHO expert advisory panels, as well as others identified through open calls for specialists. The group included program managers and other professionals involved in healthcare processes. No representatives from commercial organizations were included, as such individuals are prohibited from being members of any WHO guideline group. External resource persons, including subject matter experts and specialists in systematic reviews and GRADE methodology, were invited to the NUGAG meetings as observers to provide technical input. These individuals did not participate in decision-making processes. NUGAG’s role was to advise WHO on selecting outcomes important for decision-making and interpreting the evidence. An External Expert and Stakeholder Panel was formed during the planning stages of guideline development. This panel was consulted on the scope of the guideline, specific research questions to be addressed, and outcomes to be investigated in systematic literature reviews. The panel later reviewed and provided feedback on the completed draft guideline (Annex 6). During consultations on both the scope and draft guideline documents, an open call was issued for all interested parties to join the panel. The panel included individuals who responded to direct solicitations based on their expertise and interest in the subject matter or to WHO’s open call for public comment, which was disseminated through WHO and Codex Alimentarius Commission mailing lists and websites. WHO developed an initial set of questions to be addressed in the guideline, based on the needs of Member States and international partners for policy and program guidance, as well as a request from the Codex Committee on Nutrition and Foods for Special Dietary Uses. These questions were structured using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Control, and Outcomes) format (Annex 7). The draft PICO questions were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat and Steering Committee for Nutrition Guideline Development and made available for public comment from February 1 to February 28, 2011. Feedback from 16 individuals or organizational stakeholders was incorporated into the questions. The finalized PICO questions were presented to the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health during its March 14–18, 2011 meeting, where the guideline topic and scope were finalized. The subgroup ranked the importance of outcomes and populations, which defined the scope of evidence to be used in guideline development. Following the meeting, WHO reviewed the scientific literature and conducted new systematic reviews and meta-analyses to address the PICO questions. External experts with subject matter expertise and proficiency in systematic reviews and GRADE methodology supported these reviews. A follow-up meeting of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health was held from November 29 to December 2, 2011. During this meeting, WHO presented the systematic reviews, a draft recommendation, and GRADE evidence profiles assessing the quality of evidence. The subgroup discussed the evidence, GRADE assessments, and draft recommendation, reaching consensus on the recommendation. The systematic reviews and GRADE evidence profiles for critical outcomes formed the evidence base for drafting the guideline. The strength of each recommendation was classified based on the desirable and undesirable effects, overall quality of evidence, values and preferences in different settings, and the cost of implementation (Annex 8). The classification was discussed among NUGAG members, external resource persons, and WHO Secretariat members present at the meeting. The final wording and strength of the recommendations were determined by consensus among NUGAG members and the WHO Secretariat, with no strong disagreements reported. From February 1 to February 29, 2012, a draft of the guideline was made available for public comment. Members of the External Expert and Stakeholder Panel were consulted, and other interested parties were invited to provide feedback. Over 165 comments were received from 30 individuals and stakeholder representatives. WHO reviewed the comments and updated the guideline accordingly. The finalized guideline was presented to the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health during their March 27–30, 2012 meeting and subsequently submitted for WHO clearance before publication. In accordance with WHO’s rules, all experts participating in WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before participating. Declarations of interest forms for all guideline group members were reviewed by WHO when finalizing the composition of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health. All NUGAG members, external experts, and special invitees submitted declarations of interest forms and their curricula vitae. Additionally, participants verbally declared interests at the beginning of each meeting. WHO strictly adhered to its guidelines for managing conflicts of interest, and potential interests declared by subgroup members and external experts are summarized in Annex 9. This guideline is based on a review of epidemiological literature, including three new systematic reviews conducted by WHO to summarize evidence on potassium intake and health outcomes. The systematic reviews addressed the effects of increased potassium intake compared to lower intake on health outcomes in adults and children. Evidence was considered conclusive if the point estimate suggested a benefit or harm and the 95% confidence interval did not overlap a threshold of relevance. If the confidence interval values were not clinically relevant, the evidence was considered inconclusive. A systematic review on potassium intake and cardiovascular outcomes found limited evidence directly linking potassium consumption to all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, stroke, and coronary heart disease. In children, limited high-quality evidence was available. Four studies met inclusion criteria, with three being controlled trials conducted in the USA. Due to the limited data in children, evidence from adult studies was used to infer the effects of potassium intake on children’s health outcomes. The recommendations apply to all individuals, except those with impaired urinary potassium excretion.
